text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The words of Amos, who was among the herdsmen. Abarbanel here objects to the position of the Guide (II:32), who established as a fundamental principle that prophecy can rest only upon a person who is prepared for it, whether through natural preparation according to the constitution of his body and brain and the power of his imagination, or through the study of wisdom and the perfection of his moral qualities. Abarbanel says that this opinion is based upon the words of the philosopher, according to whom prophecy is a natural phenomenon that comes to a person like other natural forms, which do not rest upon their subjects except after the appropriate preparations have been made. But this is not the view of our Torah, for prophecy is not a natural phenomenon, nor is preparation necessary for it; rather, prophecy is necessarily miraculous. For every faculty of apprehension has a fixed and limited relationship to the thing apprehended by it, whereas the human soul has no relationship or proportion to the Divine order that would enable it to receive that order naturally, except by way of a miracle. Accordingly, natural preparations arising from one's constitution, as well as the study of wisdom, are not conditions for prophecy. Indeed, Amos, though he was among the sheep herders—for the owner of sheep is called a noked—was "among the nokdim," meaning that he served the sheep owners. He had not studied wisdom, nor did he possess honor or wealth, and nevertheless he prophesied. In my opinion, however, there is a distinction between a prophet who prophesies for his own sake and perfection, and a prophet who is sent as a messenger for the sake of the community. For God to grant prophecy to a person who is not prepared for it is like creating something from nothing, and God will not do this except for a great necessity. For all the miracles that God performed involved the creation of something from something through the transformation of forms, as I have explained elsewhere. Therefore, God will not choose to bestow the spirit of prophecy upon a person unless he is prepared for it; He then adds His blessing to the preparation already present within him, with greater strength and greater power, in order to perfect him. As our Sages said, "The Holy One, blessed be He, gives wisdom only to one who already possesses wisdom." But when God needs to send a prophet to a generation and no person can be found who is naturally prepared for this from birth, from the womb, from conception, and through his upbringing, He will choose the person whom He brings near to Himself because of his righteousness, and the miracle will be greater. Amos's prophecy was of this kind. He did not prophesy for his own sake, but rather for the sake of the community. Although three other prophets also prophesied during that period, God desired that two prophets prophesy specifically to the Ten Tribes—Hosea and Amos—and that two prophesy to Judah—Micah and Isaiah. He desired that the former two be from among the Ten Tribes: Hosea was from the tribe of Reuben, and Amos was from Tekoa, which is in the territory of Asher. At that time, He found no one among them who was more prepared for prophecy relative to the rest of the people. Since it was necessary to send him on a mission concerning the community as a whole, He added blessing and an influx of holiness to the small degree of preparation that He found within him and poured out His spirit upon him. As for Abarbanel's objection that prophecy is not found among the nations of the world, nor among Israel after the destruction of the Temple, even though it is impossible that no person prepared for prophecy should be found, this is no objection. From Maimonides' statement that only one who is prepared for prophecy can prophesy, we cannot infer that everyone who is prepared for prophecy must necessarily prophesy. For the resting of prophecy even upon one who is prepared for it depends upon the Divine will. Even one who is prepared for prophecy is not prepared for it in the manner of things that necessarily occur by nature. The prophecy of a prepared person is itself a miracle and a wonder; it is merely not as great a miracle as the prophecy of one who is unprepared. Similarly, the miracle in which God sends such blessing upon the seed of the earth that one year's produce yields grain sufficient for three years is not as great a miracle as Elisha's miracle, in which the small amount of oil in the jar filled all the vessels. Now, concerning the words, "which he saw concerning Israel," Abarbanel asks: Did he not also prophesy concerning Judah and several other nations? And why does Scripture mention the earthquake? And why does the prophecy begin, "And he said: Hashem will roar from Zion," and afterward say, "Thus says Hashem"? This does not appear to follow the usual style of prophetic expression. In my opinion, the words "And he said: Hashem will roar from Zion" continue the description of Amos. That is, the meaning is: This is Amos, who saw concerning Israel and said that "Hashem will roar from Zion." For Amos was not prepared for prophecy, nor was he established in the eyes of the people as a prophet. This was so both because of who he was—a man among the herdsmen, a shepherd of sheep and a dresser of sycamore trees—and because of his place of origin, since he was from Tekoa, where there were no disciples of the prophets and no prophet who could ordain him and testify concerning him that he was a true prophet. Nevertheless, he became established as a true prophet because, two years before the earthquake, he prophesied and said in his prophecy that "Hashem will roar from Zion," referring to the earthquake that would come from Zion. Likewise, at that time he prophesied concerning the cessation of rainfall that would occur then, as it is written, "and the pastures of the shepherds shall mourn." He prophesied this two years before the earthquake, and his prophecy came to pass two years after he had uttered it. Through this, all Israel knew that he was a trustworthy prophet of Hashem. (As for the statement that he prophesied in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, I explained at the beginning of Hosea that two years before the earthquake, Uzziah was subordinate to the kings of Israel, and the kingdom was therefore called by the name of the kingdom of Israel. This is why Jeroboam is mentioned; see there.)
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And he said. I have already explained that the meaning of the verse is: "which he saw and said two years before the earthquake." At that time, he prophesied concerning the earthquake: "Hashem will roar from Zion," for the earthquake began in Zion, and there was a great roaring there; "and from Jerusalem He will give forth His voice," which is less powerful than a roar, for the earthquake spread from Zion to Jerusalem and from there to all the cities of the Land of Israel. He gave forth His mighty voice—the sound of the earthquake that shook the earth from its place and caused its pillars to tremble. This was one prophecy that he uttered before its fulfillment. A second prophecy announced that there would be a year of drought, so severe that "the pastures of the shepherds shall mourn," for there would be no pasture for the animals, "and the summit of Carmel shall wither," though it is always filled with fresh produce. All this he prophesied two years beforehand, and when his prophecy was fulfilled, he became established as a trustworthy prophet.
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem. After describing the characteristics of the prophet and how he became established as a trustworthy prophet, the main body of the book begins. Before beginning his prophecies concerning Judah and the Ten Tribes, he first introduces prophecies of punishment against the neighbors of the Land of Israel who had harmed Israel, and announces that God would punish them for this. For although Israel was punished for its sins, nevertheless, all those who harmed them would not go unpunished, as it is written, "And also the nation whom they shall serve, I will judge." Now Aram was a neighbor of the Land of Israel to the east, the Philistines to the west, Tyre to the north, and Edom, Ammon, and Moab to the south, and he announces their punishments one after another. He begins with Aram, because they were the first to harm Israel, from the days of Elisha until the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, as explained in the Book of Kings. He said, "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, shall I not requite him?" After they committed three transgressions, and then the fourth transgression as well, must I not necessarily punish them and repay them for their deeds? But what are these three transgressions? Radak explains that they refer to the three times that they had previously harmed Israel. Abarbanel explains that they refer to the three well-known transgressions—idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed—which existed among them. Thus, He says: Although I did not repay them for the three transgressions, now that they have committed a fourth transgression as well, shall I not requite them? And the fourth transgression was "because they threshed Gilead with threshing sledges of iron." They passed iron implements over their bodies, just as grain is threshed, torturing them with cruel fury and an outpouring of wrath.
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will send a fire, for their punishment will not come in the natural manner, in which the enemy first conquers the surrounding cities of the countryside, then conquers the gate of the city, and afterward destroys the king's palace; rather, it will be the reverse. First, I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which is the royal house, and afterward it shall consume the palaces of Ben-hadad, the son of Hazael, who reigned after him and built palaces around his father's house, and afterward.
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will break the bar of Damascus, the bar of the city's fortress, and afterward I will cut off the inhabitant from the Valley of Aven, who were around Damascus, and the one who holds the scepter from Beth-eden, who belonged to the kingdom of Aram and had a governing scepter of their own under the kingdom of Aram; and they too shall go into exile with Aram to Kir, even though they were a separate tribe, so that they will resemble a dangerously ill person whose illness begins in the heart, from which the sources of life flow, and spreads from there to all the limbs of the body.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem. Now he prophesied concerning the Philistines, who were neighbors of the Land of Israel to the west. For three transgressions of Gaza, namely idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, which were in their hands, and for four, which they have now added, shall I not repay them? Because they carried away an entire exile to deliver them over to Edom. At the time of the destruction, Edom stood at the crossroads to cut down those who escaped, as it is written in Obadiah, and many fled westward through the land of the Philistines; but they delivered them into the hands of the Edomites, handing them over to the enemy so that the exile would be complete and no one would escape.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza. Gaza was fortified with a strong wall, and the wall was conquered, and the city was given over to the consuming fire.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod. There the inhabitants were cut off, while from Ashkelon the government was cut off, and Ekron was destroyed twice; therefore, He says, "And I will turn My hand against Ekron." Gath is not mentioned because it belonged to Judah.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem. He prophesies concerning Tyre, because they delivered an entire exile over to Edom. Israel trusted in the covenant that Tyre had maintained with Israel since the days of David and Solomon and fled to Tyre, but they delivered them into the hands of the Edomites (although they did not themselves carry them into exile, as the Philistines did), contrary to the commandment, "You shall not deliver a slave to his master." Their sin was great because they did not remember the covenant of brothers that they had with Israel, for Hiram said to Solomon, "What are these cities that you have given me, my brother?"
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will send a fire, for it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar and afterward by Alexander the Macedonian, as explained in Ezekiel.
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem: For three transgressions of Edom, idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, and for four, etc., because he pursued his brother with the sword at the time of the destruction of the First Temple, and his anger tore perpetually, through the Romans who destroyed Jerusalem, for the Romans were considered descendants of Edom according to what Abarbanel explained with proofs, and likewise the anger they bore toward Israel throughout the entire period of exile. There is a distinction between anger (af) and wrath (evrah): wrath is when, because of his anger, one passes beyond the proper limit to do harm to the community as a whole, including even those who have not sinned. Now the descendants of Edom have a general wrath against the entirety of Israel because of their faith, and this they preserve in their hearts forever, seeking vengeance against the entire people, to confound and destroy them, and because of this they decreed upon them slaughter, forced conversion, and destruction in every generation.
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will send a fire upon Teman, which is part of Edom, and it shall consume the palaces of Bozrah, which is the metropolis of Edom, under which is the city of Rome, concerning which Isaiah prophesied, "Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimsoned garments from Bozrah?" etc., as I explained there.
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, as stated above, and for four, etc., because they split open the mountains of Gilead. Abarbanel explains the word harot as relating to har, "mountain": because the children of Ammon were situated near the land of Gilead, they split open the neighboring mountains in order to enlarge their border. Rashi, of blessed memory, explains harot according to its plain meaning, as referring to pregnant women, whom they split open in order to eradicate Israel from there. According to both explanations, we can understand what Jeremiah said concerning the children of Ammon: "Does Israel have no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has their king inherited Gad, and his people dwelt in its cities?" The words "Why then has he inherited?" allude to the eradication of the children who would have been the heirs, while "and his people dwelt in its cities" alludes to what is written here: "in order to enlarge their border."
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will kindle. He will kindle among them the fire of war, and kindling refers to a burning that takes place all at once on every side, for the fire spread throughout all the children of Ammon. Likewise, Jeremiah said, "And her daughters shall be kindled with fire." This will be with a shout on the day of battle, and this same expression is also used there in Jeremiah. And because the worship of Milcom was the worship of fire, he says that the fire will not come from Milcom, for:
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Their king shall go into exile, and by "their king" he includes both the worship of Molech and the king in its literal sense, and therefore it says, "he and his princes."
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: For three transgressions of Moab. Abarbanel explains that he began his prophecy with Damascus, who fought against Gilead with fierce cruelty, and afterward with Gaza and Tyre, who aided Edom, and afterward with Edom itself, who harmed Israel. After this, he prophesied that He would punish the nations that had been the cause of all this. The children of Ammon were the cause of the evil committed by Damascus, for they were the first to wage war against Gilead and seize its territory, and thereby Damascus was emboldened to follow after them to destroy and annihilate. And the cause of the evil committed by the children of Edom, whom Philistia and Tyre followed, was that they burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime. For Edom had been in a covenant with Israel, and in the days of Jehoram and Jehoshaphat, Edom went with them to fight against Moab. At that time, the king of Moab captured the firstborn son of the king of Edom, who was destined to reign after him (and therefore he is called here the king of Edom), offered him as a burnt offering upon the wall, and burned him into lime. There it is written, "And there was great wrath against Israel," meaning that Edom then became enraged against Israel for not saving him from the hand of the king of Moab. From that time onward, Edom began to wage war against Israel, as it is written (II Kings 8:16) that in the days of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat (who became king in the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab), Edom rebelled from under the rule of Judah. From then onward, Edom began to harm Israel and maintained an everlasting enmity against them. Moab was the cause of this and was therefore punished. Concerning this it says (Jeremiah 48:35), in the prophecy of Moab's downfall, "And I will put an end in Moab to him who offers upon the high place and burns incense to his god," this being measure for measure.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will send, and it shall consume the palaces of Kerioth, the fortified cities of Moab, and Moab shall die amid tumult, meaning that he will not fight at all, but merely upon hearing the sound of the tumult and the battle cry, he will die from overwhelming fear. He adds that he will die upon hearing the sound of the shofar, and will not muster the strength to fight at all, as it is written (Jeremiah 48:39), "How Moab has turned his back in shame! And Moab shall become a laughingstock and a terror to all those around him."
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: (4–5) Thus says Hashem. Although I have punished all the nations that harmed Israel, I will also punish Judah. For three transgressions of Judah, namely idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, which were among them, and for four, etc., because they rejected the Torah of Hashem, and as a result, they did not keep His statutes. Their failure to keep His statutes was not because of the evil inclination or desire, but rather because of their denial and their rejection of the Torah. The cause of this was that their falsehoods led them astray, namely the false beliefs that they held concerning matters of faith. Although these beliefs were falsehoods, they held fast to them because their fathers had followed after them, and they became established among them as an inherited possession passed down from fathers to sons. Therefore, they too will receive their punishment: And I will send a fire upon Jerusalem.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem: For three transgressions of Israel, namely the Ten Tribes, who sinned through idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, and for four. The fourth sin was an addition to each of the three transgressions, for in each one they increased the sin in both its severity and its extent and combined other sins with it. Thus, regarding the sin of bloodshed, they added that they sold the righteous for silver, for because of money they had received, they sold the righteous man in his judgment to be put to death—whether the judges through bribery or false witnesses who testified that he had committed a capital offense because they had taken money. And not even for a large amount of money, for they also sold the poor to be put to death for a pair of shoes; for a pair of shoes they gave false testimony against him, and the judges sentenced him to death in return for the bribe of a pair of shoes.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Who pant. And who hired the false witnesses and gave the bribe? This was done by those who pant and lust after the dust of the earth, to take the dust of the poor man's land, meaning the small plot of land that he possesses. And this they take upon the heads of the poor, together with the heads of the poor themselves, for by cutting off his head and killing him, they will take the dust of his land. Therefore, they hire false witnesses and corrupt judges against him, and thereby they turn aside the way of the humble, perverting their way in order to sentence them to death and murder them, for bloodshed is a trivial matter in their eyes. And regarding sexual immorality, a man and his father go to the betrothed maiden, which demonstrates the extreme extent of the breach and their lack of shame before their parents in this, in order to profane My holy name.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And upon. And regarding idolatry, upon garments taken in pledge they recline beside every altar. They take the garments of the poor as pledges and dedicate them to the altar of Baal, spreading them beside the altar and reclining upon them while eating from the sacrifices offered to their idols. Likewise, the wine that they drink in the house of idolatry in honor of the idols (as it is written, "Who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their libations") is the wine of those who have been fined, for they take money from righteous people whom they have punished with monetary fines and use it to drink wine for idolatry. Thus, the sin of idolatry is combined with the sins of robbery, plundering the poor, and the groaning of the destitute.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And I. Behold, in His goodness, Hashem made preparations so that they would not defile themselves with these abominations, namely idolatry and sexual immorality, and there were two such preparations. First, He destroyed the Amorite before them, so that Israel would not learn from them to commit such abominations, as it is written at the beginning of the section concerning forbidden sexual relations, "Like the practice of the land of Egypt, etc.," and "Like the practice of the land of Canaan you shall not do." And the Sifra explains (sec. 131) that the Egyptians, and especially the place where Israel had lived among them, as well as the Amorites, and especially the places that Israel conquered, were corrupt in all these abominations. Therefore, He brought them out of Egypt and destroyed the Amorites so that Israel would not learn from their deeds. And as it is written in the Torat Kohanim, He arranged that the guilty generation would be there when Israel came, so that Israel might exact punishment from them, as I explained there. If so, how can you now make yourselves abominable through those very abominations on account of which I destroyed the Amorite? And do not say that the Amorite was destroyed through natural means and through conquest because Israel was stronger than they were. This was not so, for his height was like the height of cedars in kingship and dominion, and he was strong as the oaks in strength and might. The height also signifies their heavenly prince, for their celestial order and fortune were exalted and prosperous at that time; and he himself was strong and mighty, possessing fortified strongholds and valiant warriors. The destruction itself was also beyond the course of nature, for I destroyed his fruit from above and his roots from beneath, so that both the fruit and the roots were wiped out, and every remembrance of them was lost.
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And I. And for this purpose as well, I brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you through the wilderness for forty years, because there remained in their hearts corrupt thoughts that they had learned from the Egyptians, and He could not bring them immediately to inherit the land of the Amorite, for He feared that they might return to committing the abominations of Egypt, as it is written, "For you know how we dwelt in the land of Egypt, and you saw their abominations, etc." Therefore, He caused them to wander for forty years in the wilderness, until the previous generation died in the wilderness and the new generation witnessed the deeds of Hashem and His Providence and was refined and purified in the wilderness (as I explained in Artzot HaShalom, Discourse 2, on the verse "These are the journeys of the children of Israel"). If so, I surely made preparations so that you would not defile yourselves through idolatry, sexual immorality, and the abominations of Egypt and Canaan.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And I raised up. I made a second preparation for this purpose: in order to prevent you from being drawn after idolatry, I raised up prophets from among your sons, for the prophet was attached to the spirit of Hashem without any intermediary, and by seeing prophecy dwelling among them, they knew that Hashem watched over them without an intermediary. Thus, they had no need to consult the dead or the sun images in order to learn the future from them, as it is written, "There shall not be found among you one who makes his son or his daughter pass through fire, one who practices divination, etc.; for these nations whom you are dispossessing listen to soothsayers and diviners, but as for you, Hashem your God has not permitted you to do so. A prophet from among you, from your brethren, etc." And in order to separate them from sexual immorality, I raised up Nazirites from among your young men, for the purpose of Nazirite abstinence is to separate oneself from sexual immorality, as it is said: Why is the passage concerning the suspected adulteress placed next to the passage concerning the Nazirite? Because whoever sees a suspected adulteress in her disgrace should abstain from wine. Is this not even so, O children of Israel? That is, not only did you fail to keep My commandments and sin through idolatry and sexual immorality, but will you even nullify the very preparations intended to protect you from these sins? To the point that even this is no longer among you—neither prophets nor Nazirites, through whom faith in Hashem and abstention from sexual immorality would spread throughout the nation—for:
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And you gave the Nazirites wine to drink, so that there would be no one to teach the path of abstinence, and you commanded the prophets, saying, "Do not prophesy," so that the spirit of My holiness would not be found in Israel, nor anyone who sought the true faith and warned against idolatry. Therefore:
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, I will press you down in your place. Just as a wagon that is full of sheaves is fitted with a surrounding frame so that the sheaves will not fall out, and the sheaves are pressed together and confined within the wagon by that frame so that they cannot fall out, so I will surround you, and you will not be able to leave your place to escape the sword of the enemy.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And escape shall perish. You will be able neither to flee, for escape shall perish from the swift, nor to stand in battle against the enemy, for even one who is naturally strong shall not strengthen his power; his strength will not remain firm, for weakness of strength and faintness of heart will overcome him, and he will be unable to fight. And as for the mighty man, not only will he be unable to fight and defeat the enemy, but his might will not even avail him to save his life, at least, and rescue himself from death by escaping through his might.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And he who grasps the bow. Although at times the archers will stand against the enemy and hold him back for a short while, so that in the meantime the swift-footed man can flee, now he who grasps the bow shall not stand at all, but will immediately flee, and consequently the swift of foot shall not escape. That is, the one who grasps the bow will not, by standing against the enemy, enable the swift-footed man to escape by giving him time to flee, for he will not stand at all. And even the rider of the horse shall not save his life, although escape is easier for them.
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And the stout-hearted among the mighty. Even if there should be found among the mighty one whose heart is more courageous than all the others, his courage will avail him only in that he shall flee naked on that day and save his life by fleeing, not by fighting, nor will he save his possessions or his clothing.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear, etc., whom I brought up from the land of Egypt, and thereby I acquired you as My portion, so that you would not be under the heavenly princes and the celestial order, for My Providence is attached to you, and therefore:
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: You alone have I known from all the families of the earth. There is no other family on earth to whom My knowledge and Providence are attached as they are to you, for all the others are subject to the order of nature and the governance of the heavenly host, and therefore they are not commanded against associating other powers with God, as it is written, "which Hashem has apportioned to all the peoples under the heavens," and, "But you Hashem took and brought out of the iron furnace, from Egypt, to be His people, an inheritance." Therefore, I will visit upon you all your iniquities, since you are commanded concerning the unity of God and not to associate the worship of a foreign power with My worship, and to you were given the Torah and the commandments.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Will two walk together? Verses 3–8 are an announcement and introduction, containing the main points of the prophecies that follow from verse 9 until the end of chapter 4. He says, as a first introduction, that they should know that their punishment is not a matter of chance, but of Divine Providence, for "Will two walk together unless they have agreed to meet?" Two different people who walk together on the same journey toward a single destination have certainly been brought together for that purpose, and it is not by chance. This serves as an introduction to what he will say in verses 9, 10, and 11: since several different nations joined together to wage war against Israel, this was not by chance; rather, Hashem appointed and summoned them for this purpose, and His spirit gathered them together.
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Will a lion roar? As a second introduction, when a lion roars in the forest, it certainly has prey and does not roar for nothing. This serves as an introduction to what he will say in verse 12: the king of Assyria, who roars against them, will seize his prey, devour men, and no one will deliver them from his hand. It is already explained in accounts of natural history that when a lion is young, while it is in the stage called a kefir, it does not go out in search of its prey, but sits in its lair in ambush to devour animals that pass by it. Therefore, it says, "Does a young lion give forth its voice from its den?" But when it grows old and is called an aryeh, it goes far from its den to seize prey. Therefore, it says, "Will a lion roar in the forest?" The metaphor is that both when Assyria roared against them in their own land, and when it captured one of them in its own den—when Hoshea son of Elah went out to him and he imprisoned him, so that he was caught by him as one is caught by a young lion, for he had then entered the territory of Assyria—in both cases, there was no one who could deliver from his hand.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Will a bird fall? As a third introduction, when a bird flying high above falls into a trap resting upon the ground, is it possible that there is no snare for it? For within the trap there is a snare by which the bird is caught. Likewise, "Will a trap spring up from the ground without having caught anything?" When we see the trap spring up, it has certainly caught something. This serves as an introduction to what he will say from verse 13 onward: Israel's being caught in the hand of the king of Assyria had a cause, which served as a snare for them, as will be explained there.
text.2_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Will a shofar be sounded? As a fourth introduction, if a shofar is sounded in a city, the shofar being a sign that the sword is coming upon the land or that other troubles are approaching, is it possible that the people will not tremble? Surely they will tremble and fear the coming calamity and seek means by which to escape it. This serves as an introduction to what he will say in chapter 4, from verse 4 until the end of the passage: Hashem sounded the shofar through His prophets to warn them of the troubles that were about to come upon them—famine, locusts, pestilence, and the sword—yet they did not tremble and did not return to Hashem, through which they could have escaped the calamity. Instead, they attributed all the evils to chance. To this he responds, "Can there be calamity in a city that Hashem has not caused?" And since all calamities issue from the decree of Hashem, why did the people not return to Him who struck them?
text.2_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: For. That is, do not say that the reason they did not repent was because the decree had already been issued and they thought that their repentance would be of no avail. To this he responds that although Hashem speaks a word and issues a decree, Hashem will not carry out the evil and immediately bring it into effect unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the prophets, and He sends them to warn the people so that they will repent of their deeds and annul the decree, so that it will not come to pass. And the prophet will certainly fulfill his mission and go to warn the people. For:
text.2_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: A lion. Even if a lion has roared, who will not fear? although its roar is merely the roar of an animal; how much more so, if Hashem God has spoken, who will not prophesy? Surely the prophets will tremble, prophesy, and warn the people. Why, then, did they not repent? Accordingly, he also said metaphorically that if a shofar is sounded in a city and the people do not tremble or fear at the sound of the shofar so as to take heed, repent, and prevent the calamity, then if afterward there is calamity in the city and the decree comes upon them, Hashem has not caused it; the matter should not be attributed to Hashem, for they themselves brought the calamity upon themselves. For Hashem does not do anything without first revealing His secret to the prophets and warning the people through them; and when they do not heed the warning, the deed is not attributed to Him, but rather to the people themselves, who brought the calamity upon themselves.
text.2_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Proclaim. He begins to explain the first introduction, in which he said, "Will two walk together unless they have agreed to meet?" Behold, they shall proclaim and announce in Ashdod, which is among the Philistines, upon the palaces (for one who made a public proclamation would customarily stand upon a high palace and proclaim); likewise, they shall proclaim in the land of Egypt upon the palaces, for in the land of Egypt as well such a proclamation will be made. And say: the proclaimers shall proclaim and tell the peoples to assemble to go to war upon the mountains of Samaria. And see: there you will see that they deserve destruction, because there are great tumults within her, in matters between man and God, and oppressed people in her midst, in matters between man and his fellow. And corresponding to what he said, "for there are great tumults within her," he says:
text.2_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And they do not know how to act uprightly, in matters between man and God; and corresponding to what he said, "and oppressed people are in her midst," he explains, who store up violence and plunder in their palaces (so that even Egypt and the Philistines will be astonished at their abominations, the opposite of what he said earlier, that He brought them out of the land of Egypt so that they would not learn the abominations of the Egyptians, and destroyed the Amorite before them so that they would not act according to the abominations of the seven nations, of whom the Philistines were among them; but now the opposite has occurred, for they have become more abominable than they). And you ask: Who brought together two separate nations to join in a single plan to go against the mountains of Samaria? Will two walk together unless they have agreed to meet? Surely Hashem appointed and summoned them for this purpose.
text.2_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, thus says Hashem. Hashem appointed them, and He said, "An enemy, and around the land," meaning that they will besiege the land all around, from every side, and therefore He sent different nations against them. And he shall bring down—the enemy shall bring down your strength from you, and as a result, your palaces shall be plundered, which were filled with robbery and violence. And do not ask why we do not find that the Philistines and Egyptians came against Samaria, for in the accounts of Kings and Chronicles not all the particular events that happened to them are recorded, but only the general events. And it is reasonable that after the Philistines spread through Judah in the days of Ahaz, at the time when the king of Assyria came against Pekah (as explained in II Chronicles 28), they afterward also entered the territory of Israel, which had been weakened by the king of Assyria, as stated in Ezekiel (16:27). Likewise, Egypt had a foothold at that time in the cities of Israel, as I explained in the prophecy of Hosea (7:11; 8:9; 9:6; 11:5).
text.2_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus says Hashem. Now he explains the second introduction, in which he said, "Will a lion roar in the forest when it has no prey?" The lion roaring against them is the king of Assyria, who prepared to wage war against them, and he will seize his prey and destroy them. He explains: "As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs," for it is impossible for the shepherd to rescue the sheep that the lion has torn apart; rather, he will attempt to rescue from its mouth two legs or a piece of the ear's cartilage (so that he will have evidence that the sheep was torn apart and will be exempt from paying, as it is written, "If it is indeed torn apart, he shall bring it as evidence," meaning that he shall bring part of the torn animal as proof), "so shall the children of Israel who dwell in Samaria be rescued, in the corner of a bed," meaning that only the weak, who sit in the corner of a bed because of their weakness, will be spared from being killed or exiled. "And in Damascus, on a couch"—the meaning of the verse is: "and those who dwell in Damascus, in the corner of a couch." Upon a couch lies one who is completely ill, not merely weak; there, even the weak who sit upon a bed will not be spared, but only the sick who lie upon a sickbed. For at first the king of Assyria exiled many Israelites to Damascus, since he exiled Aram to Kir and settled Israelites in their place in Damascus; or many Israelites settled there themselves, for Jeroboam son of Joash restored Damascus to Israel, as mentioned in Kings. Afterward, the king of Assyria exiled them from Damascus as well, as it is written below (5:27), "And I will exile you beyond Damascus," for afterward he transferred them from Damascus to Halah and Habor. From there he exiled even the weak who sat upon beds, and none escaped from his hand except those who lay upon a sickbed.
text.2_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear and testify. Now he explains the third introduction, in which he said, "Will a bird fall into a trap when there is no snare for it?" Since they fell into the trap of the king of Assyria, there must necessarily have been a snare—that is, a cause through which they were ensnared and caught in the trap. He already explained this matter of their falling into the trap in Hosea (chapter 7): "Ephraim was like a foolish dove; they called to Egypt, they went to Assyria. When they go, I will spread My net over them; I will bring them down like the birds of the heavens." I explained there that Hoshea son of Elah was caught in the trap of the king of Assyria when he went to him after having sent messengers to summon the king of Egypt for aid against the kings of Assyria. In this he was compared to a bird of the heavens descending into the net; likewise, he afterward went down to the king of Assyria and was caught in his power. And there I explained that the snare of this trap was set for him by his own people, for because Hoshea wished to abolish the worship of the calves, there was opposition to him in Israel, and they informed against him and revealed to the king of Assyria that he wished to rebel against him and seek refuge under the protection of Egypt (as explained there in chapter 10 (2–6), according to my explanation there). However, the primary snare was the sin of the worship of the calves that was in their hands, and for this very sin they were punished. This is the meaning of "Hear and testify against the house of Jacob."
text.2_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: For on the day that I visit the transgressions of Israel, to punish them for their iniquities, then I will visit the altars of Beth-el, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off. This refers to Hoshea's cutting off the horns of the altar so that they would no longer sprinkle the blood of their sacrifices upon the horns of the altar. Thus, the snare of the sin of idolatry caused another snare: because Hoshea cut off the horns of the altar, a rebellion arose against him among the people, and thereby:
text.2_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will strike the winter house. The rebels destroyed the king's house, both his winter house and his summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish, which belonged to the king and the princes, and thereby many houses shall come to an end, whether through the turmoil among themselves, in which they destroyed many houses, as it is also written (Isaiah 9:20), "And the people shall be as fuel for the fire, etc.; Manasseh against Ephraim, and Ephraim against Manasseh," or because, as a result of this, they informed against their king to the king of Assyria, who imprisoned him when he went out to him. This was the snare that led to the trap, for through this snare he fell into his net, and as a result the king of Assyria afterward came up, besieged Samaria, captured it, and exiled Israel. Thus, the sin of idolatry that was in their hands was the primary snare by which the bird—Ephraim and the tribes of Israel—was caught.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear this word. He further explains another snare that they had, by which they were ensnared and caught in a deadly trap: the sin of robbery and oppression that was in their hands. This came about through their wives, women of arrogance, and therefore he addressed his words specifically to them: You cows of Bashan who are on the mountain of Samaria, who were fat and pampered, gluttonous and drunken, and who oppress the poor. That is, the oppression is attributed to them because they say to their husbands, "Bring, and let us drink," and as a result their husbands were compelled to oppress and rob others in order to provide them with wine for drunkenness.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem has sworn. He decreed their sentence against them with an oath: "For behold, days are coming when they shall carry you away in carriages," when enemies will come and carry you away in carriages with honor; "and your latter ones," meaning that in the end you will be so despised that they will not transport you in a ship used for carrying people, but rather "in fishing boats," in vessels made like pots in which fish are carried, piled one upon another.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And through the breaches. And there you will be sold to the harem, which is a place designated for women, where wives, concubines, and prostitutes are kept. And when you come into the hands of your purchasers, each woman shall go out straight ahead through the breaches; a wanton prostitute will come out to receive her, as degraded prostitutes are received, and there she will be cast into the harem to be designated for prostitution and servitude, and she will be cast through the chamber in great disgrace.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Come to Beth-el. Now he begins to explain the fourth introduction, concerning what he said, "If a shofar is sounded in a city, will the people not tremble?" He relates how Hashem commanded the prophets to sound the shofar, declare their transgression to them, and inform them of the punishment destined to come upon them, yet they did not tremble. The prophets said to them in the name of Hashem, "Come to Beth-el and transgress," etc., "and I also gave you cleanness of teeth." Just as you increase your transgressions, so will I increase your punishment. The word "proclaim" in the following verse applies to the entire passage, and its meaning is: "Proclaim: Come to Beth-el and transgress." You shall proclaim, announce, and command the people to come to Beth-el and transgress against Hashem, and to come to Gilgal, and there increase transgression even more, for in Gilgal they sinned more than in Beth-el (as it is written in Hosea 9:15, "All their wickedness is in Gilgal," and there, 12:12, "In Gilgal they sacrificed bulls"). "And bring your sacrifices every morning." Proclaim that they should bring sacrifices to idolatry every morning, and bring the tithes every three days.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And offer. And proclaim that they should offer a thanksgiving offering with leaven, just as in the House of Hashem the thanksgiving offering was offered with loaves of leavened bread; and besides the obligatory offerings, proclaim freewill offerings, so that each person will bring whatever his heart moves him to give as a freewill offering. Proclaim, meaning: proclaim and announce all these things, for so you love, O children of Israel, and all of you proclaim and exhort others concerning the worship of the calves and their sacrifices.
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: And I also. But I too sounded the shofar and decreed famine upon you, for I gave them cleanness of teeth in all your cities, so that in the large cities you would find no food at all and the teeth would be completely clean, and in all your dwelling places, in the smaller settlements and villages, where you would find various kinds of fruit, you would have lack of bread, for the various kinds of grain from which bread is made would not grow. Nevertheless, you did not return to Me, says Hashem. This is what he wondered at when he said, "If a shofar is sounded in a city, will the people not tremble?" For they did not tremble and did not return to Hashem. And now he relates that Hashem sounded the shofar five times: three times with a decree of famine, once with a decree of pestilence, and once with a decree of the sword, yet they did not tremble and did not return.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: And I also. Then I increased your chastisement with a famine more severe than the previous one, for I withheld the rain from you when there were still three months until the harvest, when the land needs rain, and as a result they sowed, but the grain did not sprout, and they also lost the seed that they had sown. And do not say that this was a natural occurrence, for they should have seen that it was an act of Divine Providence, since I caused it to rain upon one city, and upon another city I did not cause it to rain; the city whose sins were not so numerous received rain. More than this, even within a single city, one portion was rained upon if the owner of the field had committed fewer transgressions or had repented, and the portion upon which it did not rain withered. For although, if rain fell upon one portion and rainwater collected there in cisterns, they could have taken water from there to irrigate the neighboring portion upon which rain had not fallen, it would not be so, for the rain would fall in a precisely measured amount sufficient only for that particular portion, and no water would remain to irrigate the neighboring portion, so that the second portion would wither.
text.3_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall wander. And as a result, two or three cities shall wander to one city where the rain had fallen, to drink water, for in their own places there would be drought and thirst; and even then, they shall not be satisfied, for a curse would enter their bodies. Nevertheless, you did not return to Me, says Hashem. If a shofar is sounded in a city, will the people not tremble?
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: I struck. Therefore, He sounded the shofar a third time and brought an even more severe famine, striking the grain with blight and mildew, while the locust devoured the fruit of the trees; yet you did not return to Me, and the people did not tremble.
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: I sent pestilence among you. He sounded the shofar a fourth time, sending pestilence among them when they went on the way to Egypt. It is explained in Hosea that many of the Ten Tribes went at that time to Egypt because of the wrath of the oppressor, and there Hashem sent pestilence among them, as it is written there, "Egypt shall gather them; Memphis shall bury them." And also at that time, along this way, I slew your young men with the sword, together with your captured horses, for the king of Assyria came upon them on the road and slew them with the sword (as it is written there, "When they go, I will spread My net over them, etc.; their princes shall fall by the sword," as I explained there). And because they were slain by the sword, I caused the stench of your camps to rise, as the corpses of the men and horses fallen in the field began to stink, even into your nostrils, for this stench rose even into your nostrils, and through this a pestilence arose that spread even into the Land of Israel. Nevertheless, you did not return to Me, and the people did not tremble.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: I overthrew. Then He sounded the shofar a fifth time, overthrowing some among you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, referring to the exiles in which the king of Assyria exiled them from their land, so that their country was overturned and destroyed; and after the first two exiles, only Samaria and its surrounding towns remained.
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 1_Comment: And you were like a firebrand rescued from the burning, like a firebrand whose two ends have been consumed by the fire while its middle has been scorched; nevertheless, you did not return to Me, says Hashem, and the people did not tremble.
text.3_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore. After explaining what was meant by, "If a shofar is sounded in a city, will the people not tremble?" and likewise by, "Can there be calamity in a city that Hashem has not caused?" for He made clear to them that all these calamities were not matters of chance but acts of Divine Providence brought about by their sins, he now explains what was meant by, "For Hashem God does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the prophets." Hashem does not bring about evil as an absolute end in itself, for the purpose of His decreeing calamity is that they should repent through the rebukes of the prophets, and thereby the decree will be annulled and He will not bring the calamity. This is the meaning of "Therefore, thus will I do to you, O Israel," meaning that what I will thus do to you—all the calamities that have been mentioned—is not for the purpose of bringing evil; rather, the purpose of the decree of punishment is that "because I will do this to you," through your knowing that I will bring this calamity upon you, you will thereby "prepare to meet your God, O Israel." You will take it to heart to prepare yourself to meet Him and appease Him through repentance and good deeds. Do not wait until He comes upon you and brings upon you the calamity decreed by Him; rather, go out to meet Him before He comes to you and does this to you, and appease Him and return to Him so that He will not bring the calamity, for in truth, "He does nothing unless He has revealed His secret to His servants the prophets." He also alludes, by way of homiletical interpretation, to a second meaning: not only does Hashem have no desire to bring calamity upon you, but, on the contrary, His desire is only to do good and bestow goodness and kindness. By compelling Him to deal harshly with you through your evil deeds, you compel Him to act against His will, to the extent that you will receive punishment even for this—for having caused Him to do evil contrary to His desire to do good. This is similar to the saying, "The reward of a transgression is a transgression": the punishment received for the transgression is itself a transgression, and for this too they will receive punishment. This is the meaning of "This I will do to you because I will do this to you": for the very fact that I must do this to you, you will be punished, and I will bring evil upon you for having compelled Me to do evil. Therefore, "prepare to meet your God," who exercises particular Providence over you.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, He forms mountains. He brings proof of His Providence: First, from the beginning of creation, when initially the world was water within water, and the element of water covered the entire globe. We explained in our commentary on the account of Creation that initially the element of earth was mingled with the element of water, as it is written, "And darkness was upon the face of the deep," while the element of air was mingled with the element of water above. Therefore, the waters spread out and covered the entire element of earth through the expansive power possessed by the element of air, as it is written, "And the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters." Through the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He separated the element of air from the element of water so that it would exist independently, and as a result the waters contracted, the tops of the mountains became visible, and the dry land was revealed, as it is written, "Let the waters be gathered together." This is the meaning of "For behold, He forms mountains and creates the wind," for the element of earth was separated to exist by itself and the element of air by itself. This was through His general Providence, so that the earth would be prepared for habitation by animals and man. Likewise, His Providence continually watches over man individually, for "He declares to man what his thought is." Not only does He know a person's speech and deeds that are performed intentionally, but even his siach—the movements or words that escape through an emotional stirring of the soul without intention, of which the person himself is unaware—He reveals to him what he uttered through the stirring of his soul. And just as through His Providence He established nature and creation and formed the earth to be inhabited, so, when He wills, He can destroy and lay it waste. Then "He makes the dawn into darkness," darkening the dawn and nullifying the light that He created at the beginning of creation, through which He established the air (as I explained in my commentary on Genesis); this is the opposite of "creates the wind." And "He treads upon the high places of the earth," sinking the mountains into the watery depths, as it was originally when the earth was formless and void; this is the opposite of "forms mountains." For Hashem of Hosts is His name, for He rules over all the hosts of creation and all its powers.
text.4_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: She has fallen. When a person suffers a fall that is not dangerous, he rises from the fall by himself; and when he suffers a dangerous fall to the point that he cannot rise by himself, his relatives and acquaintances will hasten to raise him up. But the virgin of Israel has fallen with a dangerous fall, to the point that she shall rise no more, for she cannot rise by herself. Accordingly, it would be proper for her relatives and children to hasten to raise her from her fall. Nevertheless, she is forsaken upon her land, with none to raise her up; no one can be found to raise her, even though she is still upon her own land, she has no one to raise her. The metaphor is that in earlier times, even when they fell, they afterward strengthened themselves, rose by their own power, and girded themselves with strength. And even when they lacked the power to rise by themselves, Hashem saw their affliction and raised them up, as occurred in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, when Hashem saw the affliction of Israel and had compassion upon them. But now she has no strength of her own, and Hashem has also forsaken her, and she has no one to raise her up.
text.4_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: For thus says Hashem. He first explains what he said, that she shall no longer rise by herself, for only a few remained from many: the city that goes forth with a thousand shall have a hundred left, for nine parts out of ten of them were killed or died, and it is no longer possible for her to regain strength through natural means.
text.4_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: For thus says Hashem. Now he explains why there is no one to raise her up. Do not think that this is because the will of Hashem has changed, so that whereas He had always raised them up, Hashem has now become like an enemy. This is not so, for the will of Hashem was that they should live, and He said to the house of Israel, "Seek Me and live." Corresponding to what was said that nine parts out of ten of them had died, He says that if they seek Hashem, they will live.
text.4_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And do not seek Beth-el. Corresponding to what was said above (4:4), that they would proclaim, "Come to Beth-el and transgress; at Gilgal increase transgression," and that because of this Hashem was angered with them and struck them with famine, pestilence, and the sword until only one out of ten remained, he says, "Do not seek Beth-el," where they sought guidance from the calf, "and do not come to Gilgal," where they committed other abominations and increased transgression, as it is written in Hosea 9, "All their wickedness is in Gilgal," "and do not pass through Beersheba," for the road to Beth-el passed through there, as it is written, "As the way of Beersheba lives." He adds that they should not even travel on the road leading to the calves of Beth-aven, "for Gilgal shall surely go into exile," and from there you will not obtain life or salvation, but rather:
text.4_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Seek Hashem and live, lest He break forth like fire against the house of Joseph. Corresponding to what was said above, "And you were like a firebrand rescued from the burning, yet you did not return to Me," which was the final blow with which He struck them, and yet they still did not repent, he says that through this the house of Joseph will break forth like fire to consume even the remaining firebrand, for it shall consume, and there shall be none to extinguish it, until nothing remains of them. He also alluded to the rebellion that arose among them in the days of Hoshea son of Elah, whose cause was the calf at Beth-el, which Hoshea wished to abolish, so that two factions arose among them, as I explained in various places in Hosea, and through this rebellion they devoured one another. As it is written (Isaiah 9:18), "And the people shall be as fuel for the fire; no man shall spare his brother; Manasseh against Ephraim, and Ephraim against Manasseh." Therefore, he says that the house of Joseph will break forth like fire, for a burning tree consumes the one nearest to it; likewise, they will consume one another. Accordingly, Hashem warned them to seek Him and live, but they did not listen to His voice, and therefore He did not raise them up from their fall, for they themselves were the cause of their downfall.
text.4_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Who turn. He gives another reason why they fell with no one to raise them up: because they turn justice into wormwood. Israel can endure only through justice and righteousness, for justice encompasses the commandments between man and his fellow, while righteousness encompasses the commandments between man and God. These are the grapes that Hashem expected from the vineyard that He planted on a fertile hill, as it is written (Isaiah, chapter 5). Justice moves upon the earth to preserve civilized life, so that people may live lives that are sweet and pleasant, protecting society from oppression and robbery and enabling them to live in peace and tranquility; but they turn justice into wormwood. And righteousness takes wing toward heaven, through which the soul attains happiness, since it is a daughter of God, spiritual and Divine; but they cast righteousness down to the earth, for they regard it as an earthly, material thing of no importance whatsoever, since they do not believe in the immortality or holiness of the soul.
text.4_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: He who makes. Therefore, just as they turn sweetness into bitterness and heavenly happiness into something earthly, overturning the orders that Hashem established for their success in this world and their happiness in the world to come, so too will Hashem overturn the order of creation to confound and destroy them. He explains that Hashem arranged the order of creation in the best and most beneficial manner, for He makes the Pleiades and Orion. The Pleiades are the constellations that bring cold and water, and opposite them He made Orion, which brings heat and dryness, as our Sages said: Were it not for the heat of Orion, the world could not endure the cold of the Pleiades. They also said that the Holy One, blessed be He, took two stars from the Pleiades and thereby brought the Flood upon the world. Orion thus preserves the order of creation so that the waters will not prevail and inundate the earth. Likewise, He turns the shadow of death into morning, for He created the light through which the shadow of death is transformed into morning. But now He will turn these orders toward evil: corresponding to His turning the shadow of death into morning, now He darkens the day into night, so that the day will become night; and corresponding to His making Orion to prevent the destructive force of the Pleiades from prevailing and bringing a flood upon the world, now He Himself calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth, for Hashem of Hosts is His name, He who rules over all the hosts and orders them according to His will. And just as they overturned the order of His governance, so will He overturn the order of the governance of the world to destroy them from the face of the earth.
text.4_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Who strengthens. Likewise, because they turned justice into wormwood, the order among human beings was also overturned, so that the destroyer prevailed even over the strong and the mighty. It also means that destruction itself prevailed over them, for through their violence they were punished. And destruction shall come upon the fortress; even though the strong man dwells in a fortified city, the fortress will not save him, for destruction will come and conquer the fortress.
text.4_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: They hate. He gives another reason for their fall with no one to raise them up: because they hated those who rebuked them and sought to set them straight and return them to the proper path, whether one who rebuked them concerning justice in matters between man and his fellow, who rebukes in the gate, where judgment took place (for it was customary for judges to sit at the gate), or one who speaks with integrity, who sought to set them straight concerning righteousness in the commandments between man and God; they abhor him. Therefore, there is no hope that they will repent of their evil deeds through teachers and those who rebuke them.
text.4_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore. Thus says Hashem: Had they listened to rebuke, He would have waited for them still, in the hope that perhaps they might repent. But since there is no hope that they will repent, Hashem decreed and said: "Because you trample upon the poor," and through your trampling and plundering of the poor, "you take from him a tribute of grain." From this violence, through which you take the poor man's produce, "you have built houses of hewn stone"; therefore, "you shall not dwell in them." Likewise, from the violence through which you trample upon the poor, "you have planted desirable vineyards"; therefore, "you shall not drink their wine," for you will go into exile. This is fitting for you, measure for measure.
text.4_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: For I know that your transgressions are many. A transgression is committed out of rebellion, whereas a sin is committed because of desire and pleasure, not from an intention to rebel. Now a transgression is always more severe than a sin, since the person intends to rebel; but sins are always more numerous than transgressions, for most sinners sin because of desire and the evil inclination, while only rarely will someone commit a sin without deriving pleasure from it, solely with the intention of provoking and rebelling. But among you, the transgressions are also many in quantity, and likewise, your sins are mighty in severity. He explains what he meant by "your transgressions are many": they persecute the righteous, for when they pervert the judgment of a righteous man, it is not because of desire or pleasure, but because they are enemies of anyone who is righteous. Because of their rebelliousness, they love the violent and wicked person and hate the upright person who has been wronged and is righteous in his case, and they find him guilty even without accepting any bribe at all. Thus, this is a continual transgression. And corresponding to what he said, "your sins are mighty," he explains: they take ransom, for when they sin for their own benefit by accepting a bribe, they do not take bribes merely to pervert civil judgments; rather, they take ransom, for ransom refers to perverting capital cases (as it is written, "You shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer"). Although this is a sin committed for the sake of monetary gain, it is mighty in severity, for through it the land is polluted with blood. And thereby they turn aside the poor in the gate, for the destitute man has nothing, and his judgment in the gate does not concern monetary matters but rather capital matters, assaults, and injuries; yet they take ransom and pervert the judgment of the destitute man who has been beaten or murdered.
text.4_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore. And because you have become deeply rooted in sins and transgressions, the prudent shall be silent at that time. The wise among the people, who know your wickedness and whose way had been to rebuke you, will now remain silent and put their hands over their mouths, because it is an evil time, and they hate the one who rebukes them and kill him. Therefore, there is no one to rebuke or set the people straight, and there is no hope at all that they will repent of their iniquities, as it is written, "They hate one who rebukes in the gate." Therefore, she has fallen upon her land with no one to raise her up, for they can rise only by repenting of their iniquities.
text.4_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Seek good. He returns to his previous words, where he said, "Thus says Hashem: Seek Me and live, and do not seek Beth-el." That is, if you wish to live, this will not be achieved by seeking Beth-el, but rather by seeking Hashem. Therefore, in order that you may live, seek good and not evil. You will not live by seeking evil, by seeking the calves of Beth-el, but rather by seeking good; for by seeking good, you thereby seek Hashem, as it is written, "Seek Me and live." That is, you should seek good, and thereby Hashem God of Hosts will be with you, as you have said. For you yourselves say that you strive to have Hashem with you to save you from your enemies and your troubles, but you choose means toward this end that actually distance Hashem from you, for through the calves and violence Hashem will hide His face from you. If you wish Hashem to be with you, as you have said, then seek good, which is itself the seeking of Hashem, and this will avail you so that Hashem will be with you and you will live.
text.4_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Hate evil. He adds that not only should you refrain from seeking evil and seek good instead, but it is fitting that you should hate evil, since it is on account of evil that you are being punished, and it is fitting that you should love good, unlike what was said that they persecute the righteous, hating the good and thereby perverting the judgment of the righteous. You should do the opposite: love good, and thereby establish justice in the gate; perhaps through this Hashem will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph, granting them a remnant and hope. It may also be explained that what he said, "Seek good," refers to matters between man and God, while his additional words, "Hate evil and love good," refer to matters between man and his fellow, as it is written, "and establish justice in the gate." By seeking good in matters of faith and good deeds toward God, Hashem will be with you; and by establishing justice in the gate, Hashem will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph, for the principal cause of the exile was transgressions between man and his fellow, as it is written, "Because you trample upon the poor," etc.
text.4_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: (16–17) Therefore, thus says Hashem. Since you do not return to Hashem, there shall be lamentation in all the streets, for I will pass through your midst. This serves as an introduction to what is said afterward, "Woe to those who desire the day of Hashem." It had been received among them from the prophets that there is a day appointed for Hashem, when Hashem will reveal Himself in His glory to punish the nations that harmed Israel, called "the great and awesome day of Hashem," and that at that time Israel will be saved with an everlasting salvation. Joel had already prophesied (chapter 3), "The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the coming of the great and awesome day of Hashem." Israel desired and awaited the coming of that day, when Hashem would pass through their midst, for then He would bring all the nations down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them for the evil they had done to Israel. The prophet told them that they were mistaken in this matter, for the day of Hashem that will come for Israel's benefit will be when Israel is perfect, righteous, and worthy of salvation; but the day of Hashem that will come now, when Hashem passes through their midst, will be for them a day of darkness and gloom, for He will pass through their midst to destroy and exile them (in the manner of, "And Hashem will pass through to strike Egypt"). This is the meaning of what he says: now, when I pass through your midst, there shall be lamentation in all the streets. The rehov is the broad place before the houses where the people gather, while the hutzot are the narrow places behind the houses, where only the inhabitants of the alley and courtyard are found, namely the women and children. He thus depicts everyone gathering in the broad street to lament, while the women and children standing in the narrow streets shall answer the lamentation with "Alas! Alas!" And they shall call the farmer to mourning, for it was customary first to lament and afterward to observe mourning, as it is written, "And there they lamented with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he observed mourning for his father seven days." During the days of mourning, people cease from work, and therefore the farmers who worked the land did not participate in the people's mourning, so that they would not be kept from their work in the fields. But to this mourning they will call even the farmer, for in any case the land will lie desolate and there will be no work for them in the field. And they shall call those skilled in lamentation to wailing; for the sake of the lamentation they will call those who know how to raise a bitter cry with expressions of "Alas!" and "Woe!" to intensify the bitterness of the lamentation. And in all the vineyards there shall be lamentation, whereas until now they had celebrated in the vineyards, rejoicing and dancing in circles. All this will occur when I pass through your midst.
text.4_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: Woe. That is, since when I pass through your midst there will be for you woe and lamentation, many evils and troubles, I therefore call out to those who desire the day of Hashem, which is the day when Hashem will reveal Himself in His glory to punish the wicked: Why do you want the day of Hashem? Although the day of Hashem will be a day of salvation for Israel at the end of days, this will be when Israel is righteous, but not for you who are wicked. Although the day of Hashem that comes at the end of days will be darkness followed by light, for from the darkness of troubles will come light for the righteous and salvation for Israel, that will be at the time of restoration; but for you, it is only darkness and not light, for on that day there will be trouble and darkness for you.
text.4_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: As when. Indeed, the day may now be compared by way of metaphor to a situation when a man flees from a lion and encounters a bear. Likewise, those who escape the first exile imposed by the king of Assyria will be overtaken by the second exile. And even one who escapes from the exile, from the bear, and comes into the house and leans his hand against the wall, thinking that in his house he will find refuge from the bear, will be bitten by a snake. That is, one who escapes the second exile will be overtaken by the third exile, as it is written, "As in the former time He made light of, etc., but in the latter time He made it grievous, etc." (Isaiah 8:23).
text.4_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Is it not? If so, why do you desire the day of Hashem? Is not the day of Hashem darkness and not light? For there is in it no hope of salvation. And he adds, "and gloom," for gloom is worse than darkness: in darkness, at least the glow of the moon and stars can still be found, but in gloom there is not even a glow.
text.4_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: I hate, I despise your festivals. Corresponding to their reliance upon the sacrifices they brought to Hashem, particularly the sacrifices they brought during the festivals, He says that Hashem hates them. Now hatred applies to something that was hated from the outset, while despising applies to something that was initially chosen and afterward became despised. Thus, he says that there are festivals that He utterly hates, and even the festivals that are dedicated to Hashem, which were beloved at first, He now despises because they are sinners. And I will not smell the fragrance of your solemn assemblies; even on the days when you assemble before Me, this will not be a pleasing fragrance.
text.4_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: For even if you offer Me burnt offerings. Although on the festivals they were obligated to bring burnt offerings of appearance and festival peace offerings, and together with the burnt offering they would bring a meal offering, He says that the burnt offerings you offer Me, together with their meal offerings, I will not accept. And although the burnt offering comes to obtain atonement for the violation of a positive commandment or a negative commandment remedied by a positive commandment, it will not obtain acceptance for you; how much more so the peace offerings, for I will not even look upon the peace offerings of your fattened animals. Likewise, it says (Jeremiah 6:20), "Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not pleasing to Me."
text.4_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: Remove. And also concerning the songs that you sing during the festival when bringing the sacrifice, I say, "Remove from Me the multitude of your songs," for they are not songs of Hashem, but merely noise and clamor; likewise, "the melody of your harps," which is music played with instruments, "I will not hear."
text.4_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: And let justice roll down like water. As it is written, "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to Hashem than sacrifice." Justice concerns matters between man and his fellow, while righteousness concerns matters between man and God. Justice is implanted in the human intellect, for since man is social by nature, he requires justice, through which human society is sustained. Therefore, he compares it to flowing springs of water, whose source wells up by itself and flows outward to others; likewise, justice should flow forth and spring from the source of the human intellect and man's own nature. Righteousness, however, is not found in human nature itself, but rather man receives its commandments from Hashem. It is therefore like a stream whose waters are not found within itself but gather into it from waters flowing down from the mountains and from external springs; likewise, righteousness comes from outside man, from Hashem. And just as the waters of a stream do not well up like a spring to fill something outside themselves, but gather only within the stream itself, so too the primary purpose of acts of righteousness is the perfection of the soul itself. Therefore, he says, "and righteousness like a mighty stream." That is, the principal purpose of the pilgrimage festivals and the sacrifices was to learn there the statutes and judgments of Hashem, as it is written, "so that you may learn to fear Hashem your God." Thus, righteousness and justice are the desired purpose, not the sacrifices.
text.4_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: Did you bring Me sacrifices and meal offerings in the wilderness for forty years? He brings proof from the time when they were in the wilderness, when they did not have many animals for sacrifices or wine for libations, and the principal part of their service was that they practiced justice and righteousness, as it is written, "He performed the righteousness of Hashem and His judgments with Israel."
text.4_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall carry. He returns to what was said above, "Is not the day of Hashem darkness and not light?" For then you will go into exile, and the sacrifices and festivals will not avail you, because you will go into exile together with the idols that you made. "And you shall carry Sikkuth your king," for in the worship of Molech they made structures resembling booths, as it is written, "And the men of Babylon made Sukkoth-benoth." Likewise, they made kavvanim for him from dough, as it is written (Jeremiah 7:18), "The women knead dough to make kavvanim for the queen of heaven," for they made from the dough an image of the idol that they worshiped. Therefore, it says, "Kiyyun, your images," and through this they directed their worship toward the star to which they attributed divinity. Therefore, it says, "the star of your god."
