And corresponding to the fact that when they left Egypt they dwelt in booths, and likewise carried their dough before it had leavened, he figuratively says that when they leave Jerusalem they will carry the booths of Molech and the dough of the image of Kiyyun.
text.4_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will exile you beyond Damascus. I have already explained above (3:12) that at first he exiled some of them to Damascus, and this was not so difficult in their eyes, for Damascus was close to their border, especially since in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash it had been within the territory of Israel (as stated in II Kings 15:28). He prophesied to them that afterward he would exile them from Damascus a second time, farther away, to Halah.
text.5_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion. This entire passage continues from what is said in verse 7, "Therefore, now they shall go into exile at the head of the exiles," meaning that Israel went into exile first, and afterward all the neighboring nations went into exile, so that Israel was the first of all the exiles. This was so both in the exile of the Ten Tribes by the king of Assyria—for although the king of Assyria also exiled the other nations, as it is written, "Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?" (Isaiah 10:9), it is clear from this that he did not exile Calno, Hamath the Great, and the Philistines until after he had first exiled the Ten Tribes, so that at the time the Ten Tribes went into exile, the countries of Calno, Hamath, and Eden were still dwelling upon their land. (Likewise, we find concerning Nebuchadnezzar that he did not exile the neighboring nations of Edom, Ammon, Moab, and the Philistines until after he had exiled Judah, so that Israel was always the first of the exiles.) The prophet wonders why this was so, for according to the natural course of events, he should first have conquered and exiled the smaller and weaker kingdoms and only afterward conquered Samaria or Zion, which were mighty and fortified kingdoms. This is the meaning of "Woe," I call out: are not those who are at ease in Zion and those who trust in the mountain of Samaria secure? There is a distinction between being at ease and trusting: one who is at ease has no war at all and no external threat to disturb him, whereas one who trusts relies upon his strength even though he is at war and is not at ease. Now the inhabitants of Zion had no war at all at that time, for the king of Assyria did not come against Judah until the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, while the exile of Samaria occurred in the sixth year of Hezekiah. Therefore, he called them "those who are at ease." As for Samaria, although they were at war at that time, they trusted in their strength and in Samaria, which was a fortified city, for indeed he was forced to besiege it for three years before conquering it. If so, since the inhabitants of Zion and the Ten Tribes were mighty and powerful, and they were the distinguished of the foremost of the nations, singled out and renowned for praise as the foremost of the nations, meaning the choicest among them in stature and might, how could it be that the house of Israel came to them? That is, the house of Israel went into exile first and came in their exile to those nations, for some of them were initially exiled to the neighboring nations, as I explained above (3:12), that they were first exiled to Damascus; some passed into exile through the cities of the neighboring nations, which were still dwelling in tranquility; and others fled through them, as explained above (1:6, 9). This was contrary to the usual course of events, for the smaller kingdoms should have been exiled first.
text.5_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Pass over. He answers that this occurred through the Providence of Hashem, so that you should pass over to Calneh and see, for some of the exiles passed through Calneh during their exile; and go from there to Hamath the Great, and afterward, when the king of Assyria conquered Calneh and exiled its inhabitants, they went from there in their exile to Hamath, which was still dwelling in tranquility (as appears from Isaiah 10), for he conquered Calneh before Hamath. And afterward, when he conquered Hamath, go down to Gath of the Philistines; they passed on to Gath, whose inhabitants were still dwelling in tranquility. Therefore, Hashem providentially arranged that Israel should go into exile first, so that they would pass through these kingdoms, which, although weaker than Israel, were still dwelling upon their own land. And see: then you will perceive with your mind's eye why this was so and what caused them still to dwell in tranquility while you went at the head of the exiles. It cannot be said that this was because their kingdoms were better governed than the kingdom of the house of Israel. Therefore, he says: Are they better than these kingdoms of Zion and Samaria, so that for this reason the king of Assyria did not dare to wage war against them first? Or is their territory greater than your territory, so that he feared to wage war against them first because their land was larger and more difficult to conquer than the land of Israel and Judah? From this you will see that it was not for these reasons that he exiled you before these nations; rather, the reason your exile preceded the exile of these nations was a matter of Divine Providence from Hashem because of the wickedness of your ways. And he explains:
text.5_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Who put off the evil day. This was because those nations sought to put off the evil day and keep it at a distance, so that it would not quickly reach their borders; but you bring near the seat of violence. Through your evil deeds, you cause the cessation brought by violence to approach and draw near; you commit deeds through which the violence of the king of Assyria will quickly approach you and cause you to cease being a nation. And he explains how you bring it near.
text.5_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Who lie upon beds of ivory. A bed is made for reclining upon either by day or by night, whereas a couch is specifically intended for the lying down of women, children, the sick, and the pampered at night. They lay upon beds of ivory, and upon their couches, which were specifically intended for women's beds, there lay wanton women, namely prostitutes who were defiled by semen, as our Sages said, "They defile their couches with semen that is not their own." And they indulged themselves with delicacies, gluttonously eating and drinking with their prostitutes, eating lambs from the flock, meaning the fattened sheep, and calves that they took from the midst of the stall, where the calves were fattened and made plump.
text.5_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Who drink. And they drink wine from large bowls, rather than from small cups, and anoint themselves with the finest oils, with the best and choicest oil, namely balsam oil, but they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph, taking no heed of the distress of the community, nor mourning over the calamity threatening them and returning to Hashem with fasting, weeping, and lamentation.
text.5_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, now they shall go into exile at the head of the exiles. All these things were the reason that they would now go into exile, at an earlier time, and their exile would not be delayed until a later time, so that they went at the head of the exiles, being the first to go into exile before the other nations, because the nations took to heart the distress of their brethren and devised plans to put off and distance the evil day. And the revelry of the wanton shall cease; because they were exiled from their land, the revelry and feasting that they held for the wanton women, namely the debauched prostitutes for whose sake they held revelry and feasting every day, ceased and came to an end. Now this revelry will cease.
text.5_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem has sworn by Himself, meaning by His will, for His will is what brings everything into effect. I abhor the pride of Jacob; I no longer have any desire for the pride of Jacob, and therefore I hate his palaces, and I will deliver up the city and all that fills it into the hands of enemies.
text.5_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be, if ten men remain whom the enemy does not kill, and they remain in one house, for example, a father and his nine sons, they shall all die through the pestilence that will be in the city.
text.5_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And his uncle shall carry him. He depicts a situation in which a father, his sons, and his brothers, who would be entitled to inherit from him, have all died in the pestilence, and no relative remains to attend to the dead and bury them and to inherit the remaining house and property except the householder's uncle, as it is written, "And if his father has no brothers, then you shall give his inheritance to his father's brother." He will carry him away for burial, and he will also be the one who burns him, meaning that he will burn the bones (as it is written (I Samuel 31:12), "And they took the body of Saul, etc., and burned them." Radak explains this as the embalming of the bones with spices that burn and dry them, and particularly during a plague, lime is poured upon the bones so that they will be consumed and the pestilence will not spread from them). The reason he will carry him away is to remove the bones from the house, for since he is the heir to the house, he will wish to cleanse it of the bones. And he shall say to the one who is in the innermost part of the house, "Is there still anyone with you?" He depicts one of the household servants who has remained alive and sits in the innermost part of the house, unwilling to enter the house itself, whether because of the pestilence or because of the collapse. The uncle who is occupied with the burial will ask him, "Is there still anyone with you?" meaning whether there remains with him anyone from the household, a son or brother, who escaped the pestilence together with him. And he shall say, "None." For all the members of the household have died. And he shall say, "Silence!" Since it was customary to mention the name of Hashem over the dead, whether to acknowledge the justice of the judgment and recite the blessing "the True Judge," and also because, according to the law, one must recite the blessing Shehecheyanu as well, as it is said: If they told him that his father had died and he was his heir, he recites two blessings, "Blessed is the True Judge" and Shehecheyanu. And since he is the heir to the house, he will wish to mention the name of Hashem. Therefore, the servant will command him to be silent and say nothing, for the name of Hashem is not to be mentioned, meaning that now is not the time for this. And the servant will explain to him the reason, because:
text.5_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, Hashem commands, and He will strike the great house into fragments. Therefore, this is no time to pray because of the danger, for the great house will soon collapse. It was for this reason that he fled from the great house and sits in the innermost part of the house, that is, in the small house adjoining the great house at its rear, where there is less danger, for the small house He will strike only with small cracks, and it will not be shattered into fragments like the great house. For this reason as well, he should not sing in the name of Hashem over the benefit of the inheritance or recite the blessing Shehecheyanu, for the house will collapse and he will inherit nothing.
text.5_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Do horses run upon a rock? A rock, being a hard and sharp rocky mountain, is fit for nothing, for it is impossible to make upon it a smooth road on which horses can run in time of war; likewise, it is not fit to be plowed with oxen in order to make fields of grain upon it. This is a metaphor for their land, which has become like rock and flint, so that they will be unable either to wage war upon it on the day of battle and escape the sword or to sow grain in it and escape famine. (It likewise alludes to their hearts, which have become like rock, so that they are unable to withstand the struggle against the evil inclination or to receive the seed of moral instruction and knowledge.) He explains that the condition for victory in war is that they practice justice between man and his fellow, as is mentioned concerning Jehoshaphat in II Chronicles (chapters 19 and 20): when he appointed judges in every city, he defeated his enemies round about. And as our Sages said, the sword comes upon the world because of the perversion of justice. But you have turned justice into poison; whereas justice should sweeten all bitterness, and in an organized society people will live pleasant lives if there is justice between man and his fellow, you have turned it into bitterness. And the condition for sowing and for fields of grain to flourish is righteousness between man and God, through which Hashem watches over them and gives the rain of their land in its proper time. But you have turned the fruit of righteousness into wormwood, acting contrary to righteousness by worshiping idols, so that He shuts up the heavens and there is no rain, and the land lies desolate.
text.5_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Who rejoice over no word. Behold, concerning Jeroboam son of Joash, it is written (II Kings 14:25) that "he restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of Hashem, the God of Israel, which He spoke through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet who was from Gath-hepher. For Hashem saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter, etc., and Hashem had not spoken of blotting out the name of Israel from under heaven, and He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash." This means that Jeroboam's success at that time in restoring the border of Israel, even though Hashem knew that they were destined to go into exile because of their iniquities, was because the final decree had not yet been issued. The final decree of exile was not issued until the days of Amos, when it was decreed that they would go into exile. As I explained concerning the verse (Isaiah 7:8), "And within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be shattered from being a people," this period begins from the time when Amos prophesied, "Israel shall surely go into exile from its land," for at that time their judgment was finally decreed that they would go into exile after sixty-five years. Since in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash the decree had not yet been issued, concerning which it says, "And Hashem had not spoken of blotting out the name of Israel," meaning that He had not yet spoken the final decree at that time, and since He saw that they were greatly afflicted and that, if He left them to nature and chance, they would perish by themselves even though the time for this had not yet arrived, He was therefore compelled to save them through Jeroboam son of Joash. That generation, which heard this prophecy from Jonah son of Amittai, who told them that they had been saved because Hashem had not spoken of destroying them, rejoiced over "no word," meaning over the fact that no word or decree had been issued against them. Accordingly, they reasoned that since their victory over the enemy and the restoration of Israel's border from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah had come about not because Hashem had spoken, but because Hashem had not spoken, their salvation had therefore not occurred miraculously through Hashem. For He had not actively saved them through a word spoken for their benefit; rather, it had come about because He had not spoken evil against them, and thus they had saved themselves through Jeroboam's military power. Consequently, they thought that they had triumphed through their own strength and might, and they said, "Have we not by our own strength taken horns for ourselves?" meaning that their victory had been achieved through their own strength and might. Therefore, Hashem will deal with them measure for measure.
text.5_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, I am raising up against you a nation, says Hashem God of Hosts. The nation that I will raise against you will not come about through "no word," but through the word and declaration of Hashem God of Hosts, for now He has spoken and pronounced His declaration and issued the decree. And He will raise up the nation that will oppress you from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of the Arabah, just as previously He saved them through Jeroboam and restored their border from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah.
text.6_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus Hashem showed me. It was already stated above (chapter 4) that Hashem punished them with five kinds of punishments in order that they should repent, yet they did not return to Hashem. The first three punishments were through famine, which He brought upon them, and the final two were through pestilence and the sword. And since through all these they did not repent, the attribute of justice was poised against them to destroy them, as it is written there, "Therefore, thus will I do to you, O Israel," etc., and as I explained there. Here he relates how Hashem showed him the punishments going forth from potential into actuality, depicted in various images in the prophetic vision. First, Hashem showed him the punishments of famine, which he mentioned above: first there was the withholding of rain three months before the harvest, afterward there was blight and mildew, and finally came the cutting locust, which was the plague of locusts and the final blow in the decree of famine. Hashem showed him, and behold, He was forming locusts, at the beginning of the growth of the latter crop. The lekesh is the late rain called the malkosh, and the crop that grows through the malkosh is called lekesh. He saw that when the lekesh began to sprout and grow, Hashem formed the locusts to destroy the growing crop. And he relates that the lekesh came after the king's mowings, after the time when the king's sheep are shorn, which is in the middle of summer. Then the lekesh grew, for the crop had been delayed at that time because of the withholding of rain, and then the locusts came.
text.6_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And it came to pass, when it had nearly finished. When I saw in the prophetic vision that it was close to finishing the consumption of the vegetation of the land, and that in just a little while it would leave nothing remaining, I said, "O Hashem, please forgive." He then asked Hashem to forgive their iniquity, so that the decree would thereby be annulled, for when a person commits a transgression the first, second, and third time, he is forgiven. And this was the third punishment. He explains the reason: "How shall Jacob arise?" That is, he will have no recovery because of the famine, since he is small. Likewise, it means that he cannot rise and strengthen himself through good deeds, since he is lowly in his spiritual level.
text.6_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem relented concerning this, and through the prophet's prayer, the decree was annulled.
text.6_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus Hashem showed me. He showed him the final two decrees, which were pestilence and the sword, and depicted the decree as calling for a conflict by fire, for the sword and pestilence were likened to a fire consuming the camp, as it is written there, "And you were like a firebrand rescued from the burning." And it consumed the great deep, for it is explained there that it first consumed those who went down to Egypt for assistance, as it is written, "I sent pestilence among you in the manner of Egypt; I slew your young men with the sword." For Egypt is deep like an abyss in relation to the Land of Israel, and the prophet also describes their going to Egypt with the expression, "And you debased yourself as far as Sheol" (Isaiah 57:9). And afterward, it consumed the portion, for from there the pestilence and the sword came to the Land of Israel, as explained above, since the Land of Israel is their portion and inheritance.
text.6_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: (5–6) And I said, "Please cease." Now he could no longer say, "Please forgive," for on the fourth occasion one is not forgiven. Nevertheless, he asked that Hashem cease from punishing them, because otherwise they would have no recovery. And Hashem relented and annulled this decree as well.
text.6_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus Hashem showed me. Now He showed him in a vision that Hashem was standing upon a wall built with a plumb line, with a plumb line in His hand. In this he saw two things. First, a wall built with a plumb line, meaning a wall constructed according to precise measure and balance. This is an image of the entirety of creation that Hashem created, which is the wall encompassing all existence, built according to the attribute of justice and the plumb line of judgment. For the scales and balances of justice are extended over all existence: everything was created according to justice, and everything is ordered by the attribute of justice and general Providence, through which Hashem oversees all existence with justice and judgment. Hashem stands upon this wall, overseeing it through general Providence according to justice. Second, he saw that there was a plumb line in His hand. Although the building had already been completed, He nevertheless holds the plumb line in His hand to measure anew. This means that, beyond the general Providence established from the six days of Creation, He exercises at every moment individual Providence to punish sinners through special Providence, according to the particular judgment appropriate to the time and to those being judged.
text.6_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem said to me, "What do you see, Amos?" Since he saw two things—the wall built with a plumb line and the plumb line in Hashem's hand—He asked him, "What do you see?" That is, what in this vision appears novel and remarkable in your eyes? And I said, "A plumb line." That is, the wall built with a plumb line is not remarkable in my eyes, for I know that everything is ordered by measure and weight and according to the attribute of justice. Rather, what I see and find remarkable is the plumb line in Your hand, which You are holding after the building has already been completed. This indicates that You intend to punish a certain nation according to particular judgment and special Providence, which has no connection with the general judgment established over existence as a whole. This is what I see and carefully observe. And Hashem said, "Behold, I am placing a plumb line in the midst of My people Israel." That is, I will not leave them to be judged according to the general rule of justice, which does not look to the individual to judge each person separately, but rather judges the entire world collectively. Likewise, under general justice, sin and punishment may sometimes be passed over when the general circumstances are not suited to calamity, for according to general justice, calamity comes in accordance with the natural order and the fixed arrangement of the general governance of the world, and waits for the time suited to it according to the order of the world and the celestial configuration. But I am placing a new plumb line, a special measure that measures according to individual Providence. This differs from the general plumb line of the wall built with a plumb line in two respects: First, "I am placing a plumb line in the midst of My people Israel," to judge each individual separately through individual Providence and particular judgment. Second, "I will no longer pass over him," meaning that even if the time is not suited to punishment according to the natural order of the world, I will not postpone the punishment until a time more suited to it, but will measure out to them according to their deeds through individual Providence.
text.6_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall be desolate. Through this, the high places of Isaac shall be desolate; these are the high places that they made for the calves, and he calls them "Isaac" from the language of laughter and mockery. And the sanctuaries of Israel, namely the places they regarded as sacred at Beth-el and Dan, shall be destroyed. And I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. Although Jeroboam himself would die naturally, his house would come to an end by the sword, referring to Zechariah son of Jeroboam, who was killed by Shallum son of Jabesh.
text.6_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And Amaziah sent. Because Amos had prophesied against the high places and the sanctuaries, the anger of the priest of Beth-el was kindled, and he sent to Jeroboam, saying, "Amos has conspired against you." That is, by prophesying that Jeroboam would die by the sword, he was inciting a conspiracy against the king, for as a result the people might rise against the king to kill him, since the prophet had thus foretold in the name of Hashem, just as Jehu conspired through the prophecy of the prophet and killed his king. And so that Jeroboam would not be afraid to kill Amos out of concern that the people might contend on his behalf, he added, "The land cannot bear all his words," meaning that he speaks such things that even the land cannot endure his prophecies, for he prophesied calamity against the people as well, so that even the people would agree to his being killed. And he explains his words; corresponding to what he said, "Amos has conspired against you," he explains:
text.6_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: For thus Amos has said: "Jeroboam shall die by the sword." That is, he claimed that Amos had said this on his own authority, and that by saying Jeroboam would die by the sword, he was conspiring against the king, as explained above. And corresponding to what he said, "The land cannot bear all his words," he explained that Amos had said, "Israel shall surely go into exile from its land." In truth, all of this was false, for Amos had not said that Jeroboam would die by the sword; he had prophesied against the house of Jeroboam, not against Jeroboam himself, and therefore he had not conspired against the king. Nor had he mentioned at all that Israel would surely go into exile from its land; Amaziah fabricated this from his own heart. Our Sages have already explained that Jeroboam did not accept this evil report and did not believe Amaziah, because he had spoken falsely.
text.6_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And Amaziah said. When he saw that he could not have Amos killed by means of the king, he sought to frighten him into fleeing the land, and said to him, "O seer, go, flee to the land of Judah," for here you are in danger lest the king kill you. Moreover, you will accomplish nothing here through your prophecy. If you prophesy in order to earn your bread through your prophecy, then "there you may eat bread," for there they support the prophets with food, but not here. And if you prophesy for the sake of prophecy itself, to rebuke the people and bring them back to the right path, you will not achieve that here either; only in the land of Judah, "there you may prophesy," meaning that there they will allow you to prophesy and will listen to your voice, but not here.
text.6_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And do not prophesy again at Beth-el, not in order that you may earn your bread, for it is the king's sanctuary. At Beth-el is found the king's temple, meaning the house of the calves that the king consecrated as a sanctuary in which to perform his worship, and they will not support prophets who prophesy against the calves. Nor should you prophesy because you wish to set the people straight, for it is the royal residence, and they will not accept rebuke that is displeasing in the ears of the people.
text.6_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And Amos answered, "I am not a prophet." That is, do not think that I prophesy for the sake of prophecy because I wish to have a name among the prophets, for "I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet," meaning that this is neither my profession nor the profession of my fathers. Likewise, do not think that I prophesy for the sake of earning bread, for I have a livelihood without this, for I am a herdsman, and I have many cattle and livestock, and I tend sycamore trees, and I have a forest in which trees grow, so I have no need to earn my bread through prophecy.
text.6_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem took me. Rather, Hashem took me and chose me against my will, and He said to me, "Go, prophesy to My people Israel," for He sent me on a mission specifically to Israel, meaning the Ten Tribes, and not to the tribe of Judah, as you suggest.
text.6_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And now, hear the word of Hashem. Now, however, a new prophecy was given to him, which he had not prophesied previously, namely, that Israel would surely go into exile from its land. This is the meaning of "Now hear," for this is a prophecy that has been newly revealed to me now and which I did not know previously. You say, "Do not prophesy concerning Israel," meaning that I should not prophesy about what is destined to happen to them in the future; and even if your intention is merely that I should rebuke them and bring them back to the right path, do not preach—not even a small drop of prophecy—because they are the house of Isaac, and they will laugh and mock your rebuke.
text.6_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Therefore, thus says Hashem: Your wife shall become a harlot in the city. This is measure for measure, for when Israel worships other gods, they are compared to a harlot who is unfaithful to the companion of her youth. I wished to bring them back to Hashem, but you cause them to prostitute themselves after other gods; therefore, your wife too shall become a harlot. And she will not first be taken captive and become a harlot there, but rather she shall become a harlot in the city. For when Zechariah son of Jeroboam was killed and Shallum son of Jabesh arose, he sought to abolish the worship of the calf (as I explained in Hosea, that Shallum, and likewise Hoshea son of Elah, sought to abolish the calves, and as a result rebellion and warfare arose between factions of the people). At that time, the priest fled and died outside the Land, his sons and daughters were killed by the king, and his wife became a harlot and was abandoned to promiscuity. And the ultimate result will be that Israel shall surely go into exile from its land, for at that time the decree was finally issued. It is explained in Isaiah, chapter 7, that Amos was then told that this would occur after sixty-five years, but they did not write it explicitly because of fear, and he alluded to it with the word has ("silence"), as will be explained in the following chapter.
text.7_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Thus Hashem showed me. This too is spoken by the prophet to Amaziah. He told him that what had been said to him in prophecy—that Israel would surely go into exile—had been shown to him in a vision, for the image depicted before the prophet in the prophetic vision indicates that the decree has been finalized and will inevitably come to pass. He explains the vision that he saw concerning this: Hashem showed him a basket of summer fruit. The keluv is a vessel specifically used for placing birds caught by a hunter, as it is written, "As a cage is full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit." The kayitz are dried figs, which are ordinarily placed in a basket, not in a cage; yet he saw the figs placed in a cage.
text.7_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And He said, "What do you see?" That is, what appears remarkable to you in this vision? "A cage of summer fruit," for these two things together are remarkable: how can summer fruit be placed in a cage? He answered him that both the summer fruit and the cage signify what is destined to happen to Israel. The summer fruit signifies that "the end has come upon My people Israel." Just as the summer fruit marks the end of the gathering of the fruits and the season cannot be postponed, so too the final end has come, and "I will no longer pass over him." It will not be changed or postponed to another time.
text.7_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And the songs of the temple shall become wailings on that day. The songs that they sang in the temple of the idols will be transformed into wailing, for it was because of them that the calamity came. And the fact that they were placed in a cage, which is a vessel specifically used for placing dead birds, comes to allude to the fact that many shall be the corpses, as numerous as the carcasses of captured birds, so that they will lie in every place. Not all of them will remain in the cage, but they will be cast out from the cage, for he saw the cage empty, without birds. That is, their corpses will lie strewn through the streets. Silence. This word has no clear explanation, and it appears that the prophet had one more thing to reveal but feared to reveal it because of the danger, and therefore said, "Silence," meaning that one must remain silent and not reveal the matter. What the prophet concealed here was later explained (Isaiah, chapter 7) in the words, "And within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be shattered from being a people." This means within sixty-five years from the time when Amos prophesied that "Israel shall surely go into exile from its land," for from that time until the exile of the Ten Tribes was sixty-five years. Yet nowhere in the words of Amos do we find that he explicitly specified the time, for he was commanded not to reveal it openly but only by allusion, and it was transmitted by tradition to the disciples of the prophets. He therefore said, "Silence," meaning that one must remain silent, and he chose this word because its numerical value is sixty-five, thereby alluding that within sixty-five years, corresponding to the numerical value of has, this event would occur. The reason he did not explicitly reveal the time is that when a prophet foretells a future calamity without specifying a time, this does not greatly trouble the people, for they know that adverse prophecies can sometimes be changed or their fulfillment delayed when the people's conduct changes for the better, as it is written, "The vision that he sees is for many days hence" (Ezekiel 12). But if he specifies a definite time, this indicates that the time is near and that the event will not change under any circumstances. Hashem therefore did not wish him to say this openly, and he said the word has, "Silence," to indicate that there was a secret here about which he remained silent, while also alluding to the time through the numerical value of has. This was transmitted by tradition to the disciples of the prophets, and Isaiah, who lived in the days of Ahaz, when the time was already approaching, explained the matter: the word has means that within sixty-five years Ephraim would be shattered from being a people, and there would be many corpses everywhere.
text.7_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear this, please. He returns to what he began by saying, "For three transgressions of Israel, etc., because they sold the righteous for silver," for the final decree was sealed because they oppressed the poor and the needy. He says that those who pant after and desire to swallow up the needy, and to cause the poor of the land to cease, should hear this. They seek to have the poor cease from their labor by observing the Sabbatical year and the remission of debts, as he will explain.
text.7_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Saying. Corresponding to "those who pant after the needy," since the needy man has no field and all his livelihood comes from gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field, they say, "When will the new moon pass?" This refers to the month of harvest, during which the poor sustain themselves from the gifts designated for them. Alternatively, it means: When will the month be intercalated, so that Nisan will pass beyond its proper time, thereby delaying the barley harvest because of the Omer and diminishing the needy man's food? Then "we may sell grain" at a high price. And when will "the Sabbath" come, meaning the Sabbatical year? This corresponds to what was said, "to cause the poor of the land to cease." Concerning the poor man who has a field, they look forward to the Sabbatical year, when he has no produce from his field, and then "we will open" our storehouses of grain and raise the market price, selling as we please. Their fraud will take three forms: first, "making the ephah small"; second, "making the shekel great"; and third, "distorting the balances of deceit," which is fraud in weight through the use of dishonest scales.
text.7_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: To buy. Until the poor lack bread, and then we will buy them with silver as slaves; and the needy man, who is worse off than the poor man, we will buy for a pair of sandals, meaning for something of little value. Then we will no longer sell grain that is clean and pure, but we will sell the refuse of the grain, the waste that falls through the sieve, and even for this we will receive a high price.
text.7_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Hashem has sworn by the pride of Jacob, meaning by His glorious holy Name, upon which the pride of Jacob depended: "Surely I will never forget any of their deeds." Even if I do not punish them immediately, I will not forget, and in the end they will receive their punishment.
text.7_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Shall not the land tremble for this? That is, how can I forget their deeds? Even if I wished to forget them, the land itself would tremble from its place to swallow its inhabitants, until all who dwell in it mourn. For when people corrupt the order of law and conduct between one person and another with such depravity, nature itself takes vengeance to destroy its inhabitants. In his figurative language, the prophet depicts the calamity that will come upon them through three poetic images: first, the trembling and quaking of the earth; second, a river overflowing and covering the land. He takes this image from the Nile, which covers the land and rises because of the rains that fall upon the mountains of the land of Cush (Abyssinia). The vapors rising in the land of Egypt are driven toward the mountains of Cush, where waters pour down from the mountains and return to cover Egypt. Therefore, he says, "And all of it shall rise like the Nile," calling the Nile or because of the rains that come from the air. When the Nile rises, its waters cast up mud and mire until these settle, and then the waters come to rest. The metaphor is that at first a rebellion arose against their king, Hoshea son of Elah, as I explained in various places in Hosea. This corresponds to the earthquake arising from within the land itself. The rebels then informed the king of Assyria that Hoshea had conspired against him and sent messengers to So, king of Egypt. This corresponds to the rainwater that goes forth from the land toward Cush. As a result, the king of Assyria came upon them like an overflowing river, as it is written, "Behold, Hashem brings up upon them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria, etc." It cast up mud and mire and flooded the land, and then the land sank down when its inhabitants were exiled, just as Ezekiel figuratively says in chapter 32, "Then I will make their waters settle, etc.," because neither the foot of man nor beast was found there, due to the desolation and destruction of the land.
text.7_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall be on that day that I will cause the sun to set at noon. Now he takes up a third image: darkness will come upon their land, both from above, in that the sun will set, which is a metaphor for Hashem's withdrawal from them and for the darkening of their fortune and prosperity; and also, "I will darken the land," meaning that there will be darkness from the earth below, in the form of cloud and thick gloom, which are attributed to the earth. This is a metaphor for the confounding of their counsel and the thwarting of their might. Both will occur contrary to nature and the ordinary order of the world, and therefore he says, "at noon, in broad daylight."
text.7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will turn your festivals into mourning. During a festival one does not mourn over the past, but only over something present or future, concerning which continuing mourning can be conceived. And your songs into lamentation; lamentation is only over the past. And I will bring sackcloth upon every waist; sackcloth is worn for prayer and fasting over a present or future calamity. And baldness upon every head; baldness is over the past. That is, they will lament and make themselves bald over the past, while they will mourn and wear sackcloth over the present and the future.
text.7_Chapter, 9_Verse, 1_Comment: And I will make it like the mourning of an only child, like one who mourns for an only son and has no other son in whom to find consolation. And he adds, "and its end like a bitter day," for one whose son has died can still find consolation in the fact that he himself remains alive, but its end will be like the day of death, when all hope is lost.
text.7_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, days are coming. Corresponding to what he will say in verse 13, that on that day of exile they will faint from thirst because they did not wish to listen to the voice of Hashem, he first says that days will yet come when the famine that I will send upon the land will not be a famine for bread, and the thirst will not be a thirst for water, as on the day of exile, but rather the famine and thirst will be to hear the word of Hashem. This occurred during the Second Temple period, when the word of Hashem was rare in those days, for after the last prophets, prophetic vision ceased. Yet the Holy Spirit still remained among them, and they made use of the heavenly voice, and they sought after the word of Hashem and thirsted to hear His words.
text.7_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: And they shall wander. And after those days, they shall wander from sea to sea, that is, from the southern sea to the western sea, and from the north they shall wander to the east, for they will be scattered to the four corners of the heavens. And in all the places to which they wander in exile, they shall roam about seeking the word of Hashem, but they shall not find it, for after the destruction, even the heavenly voice ceased, together with the manifestation of the word of Hashem.
text.7_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: On that day. That is, all this will occur in the days to come in the future; but on that day of which he spoke above, when he said, "And the songs of the temple shall become wailings on that day," and, "And it shall be on that day that I will cause the sun to set at noon," namely, on the day appointed for the exile of the Ten Tribes sixty-five years later, it will not be the elders and those who seek Hashem who will thirst, nor will the thirst be for the word of Hashem. Rather, the beautiful maidens and the young men shall faint from actual thirst for water, for they do not thirst for the word of Hashem; rather, they are—
text.7_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria, by the calves made by the kings of Samaria, and who swear by the calf in Dan and by the way of Beersheba, along which they would travel to Beth-el. Therefore, they shall fall and never rise again, as he said at the beginning of his words, "She has fallen and shall rise no more." He explained the matter by saying, "For thus says Hashem: Seek Me and live; but do not seek Beth-el, etc., nor pass through Beersheba."
text.8_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: I saw Hashem standing upon the altar. It was already stated (above, 3:14): "For on the day that I punish the transgressions of Israel, I will also punish the altars of Beth-el, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off." I explained that Hoshea son of Elah sought to abolish the worship of the calves and removed the guards who had prevented Israel from going up on pilgrimage, and he cut off the horns of the altar. As a result, rebellion arose among the people, and they divided into two factions. This caused them to inform against Hoshea before the king of Assyria, who imprisoned him and besieged Samaria, thereby bringing about their exile, as I have explained in various places in my commentary on Hosea. He depicts this as having occurred through the Providence of Hashem, as though Hashem were standing upon the altar at Beth-el, and He said, "Strike the capital." This refers to the lintel of the altar-house, upon which there was a kind of ornamental knob. Through this, the thresholds shall shake, and the altar-house will be destroyed. This is itself what was meant by "and the horns of the altar shall be cut off." And cut them upon the head of them all; through this, they were all cut apart and divided into different factions, and this occurred at the beginning, meaning at the beginning of their downfall. For their end, the ultimate result of the turmoil, will be that I shall kill them by the sword through the king of Assyria. None who flees among them shall escape, for they will not be saved through flight; and even one who escapes the enemy's sword shall not be delivered, for the sword will later overtake him, as he goes on to explain.
text.8_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: If they dig down. He explains what was meant by, "None who flees among them shall escape": none of the possible means of flight will help them. If they dig a hiding place as deep as Sheol in order to conceal themselves there, from there My hand shall take them, and I will deliver them into the hand of the enemy. And if they ascend to heaven, meaning to the tops of the lofty mountains whose summits reach the heavens, from there I will bring them down into the hand of the enemy.
text.8_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And if they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel, where there were many tunnels and large caves in which people would hide, from there I will search for them and take them through the enemy. And if they conceal themselves from before My eyes in the depths of the sea, meaning on desolate and remote islands in the sea that people do not reach, from there I will command the serpent, for serpents are found there, and they will bite them.
text.8_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: And if they go into captivity. This explains what was meant by, "Nor shall any fugitive among them escape." Even those fugitives whom the enemy leaves alive and takes into captivity will not escape the sword, for from there I will command the sword, meaning that there decrees of persecution and slaughter will be issued against them. Nor will I leave them there to chance; rather, My Providence will remain upon them. But when I set My eyes upon them, it will be for evil and not for good, for I will exercise Providence over them in order to punish them with a punishment brought about through Divine Providence.
text.8_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem God of Hosts touches the land, and it melts. This corresponds to what was said above (8:8), "Shall not the land tremble for this?" which alludes to the rebellion that arose among them, while the wording there suggests that the land trembled of itself. Here he says that this occurred through Hashem. The people's rebellion, which he compared to the trembling of the land, and the enemies' sweeping the people away into exile, which he compared to the rising of the Nile and its covering the land—all this did not occur by chance, but through Hashem. He touches the land, and it melts, and the rebellion arises, as it is written, "I saw Hashem standing upon the altar." Likewise, through Hashem, the whole of it rises like the Nile, and the enemies cover it, as explained there above. All this occurred through Hashem's Providence.
text.8_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Who builds His upper chambers in the heavens. This is based on what is written: "Who stretches out the heavens like a curtain; who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters, etc.; who founded the earth upon its foundations." As I explained in my commentary on the account of Creation, at first the entire world was water within water. When Hashem willed that the dry land should appear, He stretched out the heavens like a curtain, meaning that He established in the nature of water that it should rise as vapor to the firmament, which is the sphere of the atmosphere. There, the waters that had been mixed with the air were separated and remained within the sphere of the atmosphere, as it is written, "Who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters." This refers to the law He established for the waters, that they should rise to that point and remain there bound within the clouds. Through this, the dry land was revealed and the mountains rose out of the deep, concerning which it is written, "He founded the earth upon its foundations." This is the meaning of "Who builds His upper chambers in the heavens," for there the vapors and waters ascend, and through this "He founded His gathering upon the earth," for the dry land was gathered together, and He set a boundary for the sea so that it would not go beyond that gathering. And He Himself, who restrained the waters so that they would not cover the dry land, is "He who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth," so that the world returns to a state of water within water, as He did in the generation of the Flood, when rain descended from the heavens and the waters covered the dry land. Thus, He who made it can bring His sword near to return creation to the womb of chaos.
text.8_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Are you not like the children of the Cushites to Me? After prophesying calamity, he concludes his book with words of consolation. He says: You are set apart for Me like the children of the Cushites, who are always distinctive and recognizable, and remain identified with their fathers because of the blackness of their skin. Although they may go into exile and mingle among other peoples, they do not become indistinguishable from them. So too, although you will go into exile and mingle among the nations, you will always remain recognizable, for you belong to Me. For you are the children of Israel, and all who see them will recognize them as children of the living God. He brings proof of this: Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt? Although you lived in Egypt for many years as exiles and slaves, you nevertheless did not become assimilated among the Egyptians, and I brought Israel out as a separate and recognizable people, retaining its name and lineage. But did I likewise bring the Philistines from Caphtor and Aram from Kir? This is a rhetorical question. The Philistines had been conquered in ancient times by the Caphtorites, as it is written, "And the Avvim, who dwelt in villages as far as Gaza—the Caphtorites who came forth from Caphtor destroyed them and dwelt in their place." Later, the exiles returned to the land of the Philistines, as it is written, "For Hashem will destroy the Philistines, the remnant of the island of Caphtor." Yet can it be said that I brought up the Philistines? Or when I bring Aram back from its exile in Kir, to which the king of Assyria exiled them, can it truly be said that I bring up Aram? Surely, in their exile they will intermingle with the other peoples and disappear among them, and they will no longer remain Philistines and Arameans, but will become Caphtorites and people of Kir, for they will have ceased to be the nations they were before their exile. Only Israel remained Israel and did not intermarry or assimilate among them, as it is written, "And their offspring shall be known among the nations, etc." And he explains the matter.
text.8_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, the eyes of Hashem are upon the sinful kingdom. When Hashem sets His attention upon a kingdom to punish it for its sins, then I will destroy it from upon the face of the earth; that nation will be destroyed and cease to exist as a people. Nevertheless, I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob. Although Hashem will punish them, He will not destroy their essential identity, and they will always remain the house of Jacob, recognizable by their families and their customs.
text.8_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold, I command. He explains the workings of Divine Providence in this matter: He will shake them among all the nations, so that they will wander, be scattered, and dispersed among all the peoples. This is what our Sages meant by the expression, "The Holy One, blessed be He, acted charitably toward Israel by scattering them among the nations," for through this they will not disappear in any one place, nor will any single nation be able to destroy them, since they will wander from nation to nation. Second, they will be like grain shaken in a sieve. Wheat and barley are placed in a sieve, and the sieve is shaken to cleanse them of the refuse. The fine waste falls through the holes of the sieve, but the kernel, meaning the full grains in which flour is contained, shall not fall to the ground, but will remain in the sieve. So too, through dispersion and exile, the wicked among them will fall away and become assimilated among the nations, whereas the righteous, who are bound in the bond of Torah, the commandments, and the unity of Israel, will not fall to the ground but will remain steadfast in their faith. He now explains who constitutes the refuse that will fall to the ground and pass out of the sieve.
text.8_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: All the sinners of My people shall die by the sword, for they are the refuse. They are those who say, "The evil shall not approach," meaning that they say that the coming calamity is a matter of chance and not an act of Divine Providence brought by Hashem because of their deeds. Therefore, they say that "the evil shall not approach us," meaning that the calamity that draws near will not come on our account in order to punish us, but is merely a matter of chance. And they add that it will not "overtake us," for they do not even believe that their deeds can cause the calamity to come sooner. Rather, they maintain that both the coming of the calamity and the time of its arrival are entirely matters of chance, and that it does not come upon the wicked before the righteous. This is a denial of Divine Providence and punishment.
text.8_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: On that day I will raise up the fallen booth of David. At first, the house of David was built and perfected as a permanent house, continuing through the descendants of David from generation to generation. Afterward, it was no longer a permanent house but only a temporary booth. This was during the Second Temple period, when the monarchy of the house of David had ceased and the Hasmoneans and Herod ruled. Nevertheless, there were still leaders descended from the house of David, and this was comparable to a temporary booth. Afterward, even the booth of David fell, for in this present exile the leaders too ceased to exist, and no trace of leadership remained among the descendants of the house of David. Then Hashem will raise up the booth of David, meaning that a man descended from the house of David will arise and lead the people in the manner of the former leaders. It has already been explained (Ezekiel 34:23–24) that the sun will rise for the house of David in three stages, as it is written there: "He shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd; and I, Hashem, shall be their God, and My servant David shall be a prince among them." At first, the man from the house of David shall feed them, meaning that he will lead them and compel them to practice justice and righteousness. Through this, the booth of David will be raised up—that is, leadership from his descendants will be restored—but the booth will still remain in ruins. Afterward, however, Israel will accept the kingdom of Heaven and willingly accept his leadership, and then he shall be their shepherd by their own consent. Concerning this it says, "I will close up its breaches." Through the repairing of the breaches of the generation, "I will raise up its ruins," and the booth will become whole rather than ruined, for they will willingly accept him as their shepherd. Afterward, the kingdom of Heaven will be revealed, as it is written, "And I, Hashem, shall be their God," and then, "My servant David shall be a prince among them." He will be the Messiah. At that time it will no longer be a temporary booth but a permanent structure, and therefore it says, "And I will build it as in the days of old," for the kingdom will once again be permanently established as it was formerly.
text.8_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: So that they may inherit the remnant of Edom. For most of the children of Edom will then fall in the war of Gog and Magog, and the remnant that remains of them, as well as all the nations that remain at that time, upon whom My name is called, meaning that they will acknowledge the name of Hashem and accept the true beliefs, until the name of Hashem is called upon them—all these will become an inheritance for the Messiah.
text.8_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, days are coming. He further explains that at that time the crops and fruits will become so abundant that the harvest will continue for a long time, until the season of plowing arrives, and the treading of grapes will continue until the time of sowing, because of the great abundance of grain and grapes, as it is written, "Your threshing shall reach until the vintage." The mountains will drip with sweet juice from the abundance of fruit, and the hills, where the cattle and sheep graze, will melt with the abundance of milk, as it is written at the end of Joel, "And the hills shall flow with milk."
text.8_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will restore the fortunes of My people. This means the restoration of their former stature and standing. And they shall rebuild the cities that had been desolate, and they shall plant vineyards, etc.
text.8_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will plant them upon their land. From then on, they will be like a tree planted in its place, which cannot be uprooted from its soil; so too, they will never again be uprooted from their land, for they will never again go into exile.
